scenes.title: Previously: the runtime
flow: An Agent you set up once

captions.text: Recap of chapter 15: you wrapped the loop in an Agent class.
stream() yields an Event for each thing that happens.
run() goes to the end and returns a Result.
And history lets one conversation carry on. That's the runtime.
Today's black box: what happens inside a run.
Let's open it.
A new question: which day had the most coffee revenue? We print the answer and the step count.
Predict: there are three files. How many steps will it take?
Tuesday is right. It took seven steps, though. Why seven?
We can't tell. The run is a black box.
A hook is an object the agent calls at set moments during a run.
Before and after each model call.
Before and after each tool call.
And once at the end. Every moment does nothing, until you override it.
Printer overrides two moments, and prints each tool call and its result.
The same run, with one change: hooks=[Printer()]. The loop's code stays as it was.
Its first move was to guess a file name. That file doesn't exist.
Then it recovered: it listed the folder, and read all three files.
Last, it added the numbers. Nobody asked for a total.
How does the agent reach the hooks? Through one method: notify.
It calls that moment on every hook, then returns the first answer that isn't None.
So before_tool can answer. If it returns text, that text replaces the tool's result.
That means a hook can change a run, not just watch it.
Approval asks a person before running the tools you name.
If the answer isn't y, the tool never runs. The model reads this refusal instead.
Here, the agent must read Monday's sales, then save a note. Saving needs your approval.
Predict: what number will it try to save?
It asked for both tools in one reply, before it had seen the file.
So $543.21 is made up. Monday's coffee was 120. We type n.
The note was never saved, and the model says the save failed.
Printer's output is gone when the run ends. Tracer keeps a record in a file.
It writes one line of JSON for each moment, so a trace is easy to read back.
It records how long each call took, and everything the model replied.
demo.py traces the coffee total. show_trace prints the file for a person to read.
Predict: as the run goes on, will each model call read more tokens, or fewer?
More. 272 tokens at the start, and 561 at the end. Timings on your machine will differ.
That's chapter 12's lesson as a number: each call resends the whole conversation.
Now trace our Tuesday question.
4,289 tokens. The coffee total took 2,634, and this needs the same three files.
The first line tells us why it wandered: nothing says where the files are.
So add one sentence to the system prompt: Files are in the sales folder.
Predict: will it answer in fewer steps?
No guessing now. But it makes every call twice, and runs out of steps.
We ran this four times, and got the same calls each time. Did the fix fail?
That was temperature 0. This provided tool runs both prompts five times at temperature 0.7.
Here, the better prompt named Tuesday in 5 of 5 runs. The original managed 2.
Across three batches, that's 15 of 15 against 5 of 15.
A trace shows why one run went wrong. It can't tell you how often.
Your turn. Open exercises.py, and write four hooks and a trace reader.
The checks use a fake model, so Ollama doesn't need to be running.
You've finished when you see 5 passed.

scenes.title: You opened the run.
points: Hooks watch a run from outside the loop
A hook can block a tool
A trace shows why, not how often

captions.text: Now you can see inside every run, and step in.
Next, you'll handle what goes wrong.
